Surah "al-Nas" (The Mankind)

In the Name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾ — i.e., the one who nurtures them (murabbīhim) and sets them right (muslihihim).
﴿The King of mankind﴾, their Owner and the one who manages their affairs.

﴿The God of mankind﴾, that is, their object of worship (*ma'bud*). He did not settle for mentioning the annexed noun ("mankind") only once, because his saying "the King of mankind, the God of mankind" is an *ʿaṭf al-bayān* (explicative apposition, عطف البيان) to "the Lord of mankind." "The lord of mankind" and "the king of mankind" may be said of others, but "the God of mankind" is exclusive, with no partner in it. The explicative apposition serves to clarify, so it is as though it were the place for explicit mention rather than a pronoun. The Lord is attributed to mankind specifically, although He is the Lord of every creature, in order to honour them. Also, the seeking of refuge was made from the evil of the whisperer who whispers into the breasts of mankind, so it is as though it were said: "I seek refuge from the evil of the whisperer who whispers to mankind, by the Lord of mankind, who rules over their affairs, who is their God and their object of worship." It is also said that by the first (the Lord of mankind) he meant children, and the meaning of lordship (*rubūbiyyah*) indicates this; by the second (the King of mankind) he meant youths, and the word "King," which points to governance, indicates this; by the third (the God of mankind) he meant the elderly, and the word "God," which points to worship, indicates this; by the fourth he meant the righteous, since Satan is eager to lead them astray; (p-٧٠٠) and by the fifth he meant the corrupters, because of its being conjoined to "the one from whose evil refuge is sought."

**﴿From the evil of the whisperer﴾**: *al-waswas* is a noun meaning *al-waswasah* (the act of whispering), like *الزِّلْزالُ* (al-zilzal) meaning *الزَّلْزَلَةُ* (al-zalzalah). As for the verbal noun (*al-masdar*), it is *وِسْواسٌ* (wiswas), with a kasra on the wa, like *الزِّلْزالُ*. The word here refers to Satan, who is named by the verbal noun as if he were himself a whispering (*waswasah*) in his very self, because whispering is his occupation, to which he is devoted. Or it may be that *dhu al-waswas* (the one who whispers) is intended. *Al-waswasah* is a faint sound.

**﴿the slinker﴾**: *al-khannas* refers to one whose habit is to *yakhnis* (slink back). It is derived from *al-khunus*, which means withdrawing or holding back, like *al-'awaj* and *al-batat*. This is in line with what is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "When a person remembers his Lord, Satan slinks back and turns away; and when he becomes heedless, he returns and whispers to him."

"Who whispers into the breasts of mankind" (﴿الَّذِي يُوَسْوِسُ فِي صُدُورِ النَّاسِ﴾). It is in the genitive position, as an adjective (ʿala al-ṣifah) describing "the Whisperer" (al-waswās) in the previous verse. Or it is in the nominative, or the accusative by way of abuse (ʿala al-shatm). On both of these two readings, it is good to pause (al-waqf) at "al-khannās."

**[Commentary on verse 6]**

﴿From among the jinn and mankind﴾ explains "the one who whispers," indicating that the devil is of two kinds: a jinn and a human, as He said: ﴿devils of mankind and jinn﴾ [al-An'am: 112]. It is related from Abu Dhar (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said to a man: "Have you sought refuge in Allah from the devil of mankind?"

It was narrated that "he (ﷺ) was bewitched and fell ill. Two angels came to him while he was asleep. One of them said to his companion: 'What is wrong with him?' The other said: 'He has been bewitched (ṭubb).' He asked: 'Who bewitched him?' He said: 'Labid ibn A'sam, the Jew.' He asked: 'With what did he bewitch him?' He said: 'With a comb and combings, in the sheath of a male date-spathe, under a stone (rā'ūfah) in the well of Dhi Arwan.'" Then he (ﷺ) awoke and sent al-Zubayr, 'Ali, and 'Ammar (may Allah be pleased with them), and they drained the water of the well and brought out the sheath. In it were the combings of his hair and some teeth of his comb, and there was a knotted string in which there were eleven knots, pierced with needles. Then these two surahs were revealed, and whenever Jibril recited a verse, one knot was loosed, until when the last knot was loosed, he (ﷺ) rose as if he had been released from a tether. Jibril began to say: "In the name of Allah I perform ruqyah for you (arqīk), and Allah cures you of every ailment that harms you."

For this reason, ruqyah (incantation for healing) is permitted only with what comes from the Book of Allah and the words of His Messenger (ﷺ), and not with what is in Syriac, Hebrew, or Indian (languages), for it is not lawful to believe in it or rely upon it. We seek refuge in Allah from the evils of our souls, from the bad consequences of our deeds and sayings, and from the evil of what we have done and what we have not done. We bear witness that there is no god but Allah, alone, with no partner, and that Muhammad is His servant, His Messenger, His prophet, and His chosen one, whom He sent with guidance and the religion of truth, that He might make it prevail over all religion, even though the polytheists dislike it. May Allah send blessings upon our master Muhammad, and upon his family, the lamps of mankind, and upon his companions, the keys to the abode of peace.

And Allah knows best what is correct, and to Him is the refuge and the return.
